newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Taxi shortage is worst effect of S.Korean strike.
newsitem.headline: Taxi shortage is worst effect of S.Korean strike.

text.p: A lack of taxis was the only indication in Seoul that a strike billed as the biggest in the country's history had begun on Tuesday.
Subways, buses and banks were working normally and the streets of the capital were quiet as workers ignored calls by the officially-sanctioned Federation of Korean Trade Unions for all-out stoppages.

Taxi drivers were the only workers to join with any enthusiasm strike protests against the passage of a new labour law that allows companies to shed workers, replace strikers and cut back on overtime payments by adopting flexible hours.

White collar workers planned a "necktie" rally at lunchtime and members of the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions scheduled a march on a Seoul cathedral where their leaders are sheltering from arrest.
Strikes were not even the main story on early network news broadcasts.
They were upstaged by coverage of a former Japanese cabinet minister whose defence of Japan's 1910-45 colonial rule over the Korean peninusla has sparked outrage.
Stock investors took comfort from the token response to union calls to disrupt key services and cripple manufacturing industries. Share prices rose in early morning trading.
The composite index was up 3.43 points at 662.97 in the first 30 minutes of trading.

"Investors think the impact from the strikes has already been reflected on the stock prices. Strikes are more than offset by improving market fundamentals," said a Ssangyong Investment and Securities broker.
"Investors appeared to be more interested in such factors as rising deposits amid falling margin loans, although strikes are still a major concern," said Koh Kyung-bae of Hyundai Securities.
The southeast city of Ulsan, home of the giant Hyundai conglomerate and a traditional hotbed of militant unionism, was largely peaceful.
Hyundai Motors had earlier closed down its car plants, the largest in the country, after a worker go-slow.
However, auto workers have now occupied the plants and on Tuesday held noisy rallies by idle production lines, singing and chanting anti-government slogans and banging drums.

"Down with the Kim Young-sam government" and "abolish the evil law", the workers chanted, referring to the South Korean president who made clear on Monday he would neither dump nor modify the legislation.
"We will fight to the end," union official Ha Boo-young bellowed through a loudhailer.
However, shipbuilders at Hyundai Heavy Industries were working normally.
The government argues a more flexible labour market is urgently needed to help companies cut costs and boost their competitiveness while exports are slumping.
The federation ordered a two-day stoppage by its 1.2 million members on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The legislation passed on December 26 has sparked wildcat strikes organised mainly by the militant confederation, which is outlawed by the government. Seven of its leaders are camped out in a ramshackle tent on the grounds of Myongdong cathedral evading arrest for leading illegal stoppages.
Union leaders said the impact of strikes would be more serious on Wednesday when telecommunications workers and subway and bus drivers belonging to the confederation walked out.
The confederation has called out its 500,000 members on Wednesday on an indefinite strke unless the law is scrapped by midnight on Tuesday.
